claims.claim: yellow perch in Lake Saint-Pierre, Quebec: first-winter survival high above a pre-winter length of 66–73 mm
claims.location: PDF p. 4, Abstract; p. 30 (PDF p. 44), Table 3; p. 33 (PDF p. 47), Discussion
claims.quote: a pre-winter size threshold between 66 mm and 73 mm
claims.conditions: Lake Saint-Pierre (a fluvial lake of the St. Lawrence); 2020 and 2021 year classes; total length; back-calculated from lapillus daily increments (size at 100 days, converted by a fitted model to size on the mean capture date, 9 October); survival ratio = relative frequency of survivors caught the next spring (n = 39 and 38) over that of the autumn young (n = 42 and 40) per 5-mm class
claims.note: the 66–73-mm class (index 69.5 mm) is where the survival ratio first reaches ~1 (1.47 in 2020, 0.96 in 2021; Table 3, read on the text and raw layer); the 63-mm class had 0.53–0.57 and the 56.5-mm class 0.13. It is a size class of a small two-year sample, not a fitted threshold; 'survival high above 66–73 mm' is the author's own wording (p. 33).

notes: Also useful: the thesis says Lake Saint-Pierre yellow perch need ≥ 13.5 °C to grow, not reached from October to mid-May, so their otoliths show almost no winter growth (p. 32–33); first-year length there fell from ~85 mm (1980s) to ~75 (early 2000s) to ~65 mm (2019–2020) (p. 9, French chapter, citing Magnan et al. 2022); and it relays Post & Evans (1989) as finding that yellow perch 'reaching 70 mm exhibited low winter mortality rates due to starvation' (p. 33) — a lead for the Post_Evans_1989 entry, not a confirmation of it. In 2020 cormorants took young perch larger than the lake average (not in 2019).
